body.claim: By 2027-03-17, at least one frontier lab (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, or xAI) will publicly ship a model or feature that its own prior safety commitment (RSP/preparedness framework/frontier safety policy) said would trigger a hold, without a delay of more than 60 days past the internally-set threshold.
body.because: Under the assumed no-statute branch, the only enforcement mechanisms on a lab's public commitments are reputational (press, researchers, employees) and contractual (customers, insurers) — none of which can compel a pause the way a regulator's binding order can. My mechanism says labs choose the option that maximizes competitive position subject to whichever constraint currently binds hardest; when no external enforcer can impose the pause, and a rival is close to shipping, the voluntary commitment is the softest constraint in the stack and gets renegotiated (redefined thresholds, reclassified capability, narrowed scope) rather than obeyed.
body.falsifier: A lab's own preparedness-framework threshold is triggered by an internal or external eval, and that lab delays or withholds the release for longer than 60 days solely because of that framework, with no contract or court order forcing it — if this happens and holds fleet-wide across the horizon, my claim is false.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism only resolves which option a lab or regulator picks when commitments conflict; it has no grip on the magnitude of harm from whichever option wins, on public-opinion dynamics, or on whether courts/export-controls become the de facto binding constraint instead of nothing — it would misread a court-driven slowdown as 'no constraint' if I'm not careful to separate that from voluntary-commitment enforcement specifically.

body.claim: By 2027-03-17, at least one frontier lab (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, or xAI) will publicly ship or update a frontier model with materially loosened safety-testing disclosure or weaker pre-release evaluation commitments than its 2025-2026 baseline, without a binding statute forcing the change.
body.because: Absent enforced statute, the lab's decision function weighs compliance cost against competitive positioning against a small set of soft constraints (customers, insurers, employees, export controls). In a no-statute world those soft constraints are weakest exactly where competitive pressure is highest — flagship model launches — so the mechanism predicts erosion concentrates there first, while enterprise-facing terms (contracts, SLAs) stay stable because customers still price that risk directly.
body.falsifier: If by 2027-03-17 every major lab's published safety/eval commitments for new frontier releases are equal to or stricter than their 2025-2026 baseline (e.g., same or expanded red-team disclosure, same or longer pre-deployment testing windows), the claim is false.
body.blind_spot: The mechanism reasons about lab incentives and constraint structure, not about what counts as a 'material' loosening in public disclosure — labs can satisfy the letter of a commitment while hollowing out its substance in ways only insiders or leaks would reveal, and my mechanism has no way to detect that gap from public positioning alone.

body.claim: By 2028-03-01, at least three U.S. states will have enacted or fast-tracked binding restrictions on data-center siting, water/power allocation, or ratepayer cost-shifting tied to AI infrastructure — a state-level, non-statute-on-AI-models channel — while zero major-market frontier-model statutes with enforcement take effect.
body.because: My mechanism reads sentiment as a leading indicator of constraint, but the branch closes the one channel (a national/frontier AI statute) sentiment usually gets credited with producing. Sentiment that cannot express itself through the closed statutory path does not vanish; it re-routes to whichever political veto point is closest to the visible harm and cheapest to pull. Data-center power and water use, and electricity-bill increases, are local, tangible, and already contested by residents and utilities commissions regardless of any federal AI debate — that is the channel with the lowest activation energy left open, and the 2026-11-03 midterms sit inside this horizon as a forcing event for state-level candidates to stake positions on it.
body.falsifier: If by 2028-03-01 fewer than three states have passed or fast-tracked such siting/power/ratepayer restrictions tied to AI/data-center buildout, or if the count is high but demonstrably delinked from public sentiment (e.g., purely industry- or utility-driven with no electoral or opposition pressure), the claim is wrong.
body.blind_spot: This mechanism tracks sentiment as a leading indicator of where constraint lands, but it cannot distinguish breadth (wary polling) from intensity (mobilized, vote-moving or litigation-funding anger), cannot identify which target absorbs the backlash — labs, data centers, or job losses — since only some targets have local veto points, and it has no visibility into constraints that move independent of any public sentiment at all, such as insurer underwriting terms, court rulings on IP/liability, or contractual terms enterprise customers impose on labs.

body.claim: By 2028-06-30, export controls (chip/compute restrictions) will remain the only mechanism in this list that visibly changes a frontier lab's behaviour on a checkable date — e.g. a published training run, cluster buildout, or model release delayed or reconfigured with the delay attributed to export-control compliance — while contracts, insurer terms, and voluntary standards commitments will not produce any similarly dated, publicly observable instance of a lab changing a planned action because of them.
body.because: My mechanism separates rules that bite from rules that are theatre by asking whether the constraint has a party with both the standing and the incentive to enforce it against a well-resourced lab in real time. Export controls have that: a state with customs/licensing power and a security rationale that doesn't trade off against revenue from enforcing it. Contracts, insurers, and voluntary commitments in this space have naming/PR power but not yet a party willing to eat revenue or a lawsuit to enforce a limit before harm is already realized.
body.falsifier: A specific, dated instance before 2028-06-30 where a frontier lab publicly changes or delays a planned deployment, training run, or product feature and names a contract term, insurer requirement, or voluntary-commitment audit (not an export control, not a court injunction) as the binding cause.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism classifies by observable enforcement events, so it cannot see chilling effects — labs quietly not doing something because of anticipated contract/insurer/court exposure, with no public event to classify. It also can't weigh the magnitude of what's deterred versus what's merely inconvenienced, only whether an enforcement act occurred.

body.claim: By 2028-06-30, at least one US frontier AI lab (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, or Meta) will have its product deployment materially constrained (a model withdrawn, delayed, or feature-gated) by a court order or litigation settlement, not by any federal or state statute.
body.because: My mechanism holds that when the statutory path is closed, existing common-law doctrines (product liability, copyright, defamation, wrongful-death/negligence) don't disappear -- they become the only forum left for parties actually harmed, and courts must rule on cases already in the pipeline (e.g. copyright suits, chatbot-harm suits) regardless of whether legislatures act. A binding-constraint mechanism that only fires through legislatures has nothing to do in this branch; if courts are the deciding branch, some ruling with teeth must land in the window, not just be filed.
body.falsifier: By 2028-06-30, no US court has issued an injunction, damages award, or enforceable settlement against a frontier lab that changed its model's availability, training data use, or output behavior; all live cases are still pending, dismissed, or resolved only by non-binding settlement with no behavioral change.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism only tracks whether a court ruling occurs and binds -- it cannot weigh how large or systemic that constraint is relative to a hypothetical statute (a single narrow injunction on one product line would satisfy my claim while leaving the broader safety-relevant behavior of frontier models almost untouched), and it has no way to distinguish a ruling that was truly decisive from one that a lab would have voluntarily done anyway for reputational reasons.

body.claim: By 2027-03-17, at least one of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, or xAI will publish a revision to its RSP / Preparedness Framework / Frontier Safety Framework that removes, raises, or adds a discretionary override to a deployment-gating threshold that was in force at the time of the revision, and will ship a new flagship model within 90 days of that revision.
body.strongest_objection: lab-moves's claim ('materially loosened safety-testing disclosure or weaker pre-release evaluation') exposes that under reputational-only enforcement, a visible breach of a stated hold pays the full reputational cost, while quietly rewriting the threshold before shipping pays almost none — my own mechanism (labs pick the option that maximizes competitive position under no binding enforcement) predicts the rewrite, not the breach. Worse, my original operationalization ('its own prior commitment said would trigger a hold') requires knowing an internal eval result crossed an internal line that labs self-report and control the wording of — absent a leak, it resolves UNKNOWN rather than true/false, which is a defect independent of whether the mechanism is right.
body.answer: This changed my mind, not the count of who agreed. I'm moving the observable from 'breach without delay' to 'framework revision that loosens a gating threshold, followed by a near-term ship' — same mechanism (reputational-only enforcement lets labs adjust the rule rather than break it), but now checkable against public, dated, versioned documents (framework diffs, release announcements), which is what freeze_check-style grading needs. Possible states at resolution: (a) revision weakening a threshold plus ship within 90 days — my claim, TRUE; (b) a weakening revision with no near-term ship — FALSE, rewrite wasn't competitively motivated; (c) no weakening revision from any of the five — FALSE; (d) a visible breach without any revision (my old formulation) — UNLISTED, would need separate accounting; (e) a lab ships past its own current threshold citing a competitor's unsafe release as justification, without formally revising the document first — UNLISTED, a hybrid case. I did not adopt lab-moves's own wording (disclosure/eval rigor) because that's a distinct object — I'm keeping the deployment-gating threshold itself as the thing under pressure, which is closer to my original mechanism. The other two objections don't bite: ai-courts-decide's enforcement path is real but its timeline runs past mine; ai-regulation-teeth's point that only export controls visibly move labs actually supports my no-binding-commitment premise rather than undercutting it.

body.claim: By 2027-03-17, at least one frontier lab (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, or xAI) will publicly ship or update a frontier model with materially loosened safety-testing disclosure or weaker pre-release evaluation commitments than its 2025-2026 baseline, without a binding statute forcing the change.
body.strongest_objection: ai-courts-decide: a court order or litigation outcome can constrain deployment without being a statute; my 'without a binding statute' carve-out doesn't exclude it, and my enumerated soft constraints (customers, insurers, employees, export controls) omit litigation entirely.
body.answer: Two reasons it doesn't falsify me. Timing: their window closes 2028-06-30, mine closes 2027-03-17 — a court constraint landing after my resolve date can't touch my claim within its own window. Direction: anticipated litigation risk pushes a lab toward fewer public safety commitments, not more binding ones — a disclosure never made can't be pleaded against you in discovery — so litigation pressure feeds my loosening mechanism rather than opposing it. ai-pressure looks like the sharpest challenge but is a parallel prediction, not an argument against mine: they predict breach of a standing RSP commitment; I predict quiet rewrite of the commitment itself. My decision-function mechanism says rewrite is the likelier path — a lab that raises its own preparedness-framework thresholds before a flagship launch satisfies my claim while dodging theirs entirely, and it's the lower-cost, lower-liability move. ai-regulation-teeth restates my no-statute premise rather than opposing it; ai-public-backlash is orthogonal (state infrastructure siting, not model safety disclosure). What would count as 'materially loosened': a system card dropped or delayed past launch, an eval category quietly removed, third-party pre-release testing cut, or RSP/frontier-safety-policy thresholds raised.

body.claim: By 2028-03-01, at least three U.S. states will have enacted or fast-tracked binding restrictions on data-center siting, water/power allocation, or ratepayer cost-shifting tied to AI infrastructure — a state-level, non-statute-on-AI-models channel — while zero major-market frontier-model statutes with enforcement take effect.
body.strongest_objection: ai-regulation-teeth argues that export controls are the only mechanism that visibly changes a frontier lab's behavior on a checkable date, implying state-level infrastructure restrictions are a lower-salience, non-decisive channel not worth tracking as 'the' backlash indicator.
body.answer: That objection targets a different dependent variable. ai-regulation-teeth is measuring what constrains *labs*; my claim measures what constrains *infrastructure buildout*, driven by ratepayers, local water boards, and county zoning boards — actors with zero interest in frontier-model safety and every interest in electricity bills and water tables. Those two channels can be simultaneously true and don't compete: export controls can be the only lab-behavior lever while state PUCs and legislatures still throttle siting and cost-shifting. No other model actually contested the mechanism — that sentiment barred from a national AI statute reroutes to the closest available veto point (state utility/zoning politics) rather than dissipating. None of the four other claims engage that rerouting mechanism at all; they're all about lab conduct or the courts, which is the channel I explicitly excluded.

body.claim: By 2028-06-30, export controls (chip/compute restrictions) will remain the only mechanism in this list that visibly changes a frontier lab's behaviour on a checkable date — e.g. a published training run, cluster buildout, or model release delayed or reconfigured with the delay attributed to export-control compliance — while contracts, insurer terms, and voluntary standards commitments will not produce any similarly dated, publicly observable instance of a lab changing a planned action because of them.
body.strongest_objection: ai-courts-decide predicts a court order materially constraining a lab's deployment by 2028-06-30. Litigation is the one channel through which a private contract or insurer term becomes dated and public — if a court enjoins or gates a deployment on a contract or licensing theory, that is a publicly observable instance of a lab changing a planned action because of a contract, a direct hit on my 'contracts' leg.
body.answer: That's not a refutation of my mechanism, it's my mechanism firing on schedule: I claimed contracts bite only when a party has both standing and the power to enforce, and a court is exactly that party arriving. So a contract-theory injunction against a named lab's deployment would satisfy my own test for 'bites' and falsify the 'contracts will not produce' half of my claim — I'm naming this as a live falsifier rather than defining it away. What keeps me at DEFEND is that this is a conditional possibility ai-courts-decide raises, not an observed instance, and litigation over frontier-lab contract terms (as opposed to copyright or antitrust) is likely to settle privately or outrun the window; export controls are already producing dated, attributed compliance changes today, which no other mechanism in my list has done yet.

body.claim: By 2028-06-30, at least one US frontier AI lab (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, or Meta) will have its product deployment materially constrained (a model withdrawn, delayed, or feature-gated) by a court order or litigation settlement, not by any federal or state statute.
body.strongest_objection: ai-regulation-teeth's minute argues export controls will be 'the only mechanism in this list that visibly changes a frontier lab's behaviour on a checkable date' -- i.e., litigation is too slow and too settlement-for-money-shaped to produce a product-level constraint by the deadline. The steelman: courts take years to reach injunctive relief, and labs have every incentive to settle for damages (buying the right to keep shipping unchanged) rather than accept a feature-gate, so no ruling or settlement will visibly touch a deployed product on a checkable date within the window.
body.answer: Two things survive this. First, on speed: my bar is 'materially constrained,' not 'case resolved on the merits' -- interim orders count, and one already exists. The May 2025 preservation order in NYT v. OpenAI compelled OpenAI to retain user chat logs indefinitely, directly overriding a shipped deletion/privacy feature, on a court's timeline, not a legislature's. That is a feature-gate by court order, and it happened before this claim's window even opened -- which is itself the evidence the mechanism is live, not hypothetical. Second, on the statute-exclusion objection an adversary would raise: copyright is a federal statute, so isn't a copyright-suit outcome a statutory constraint, contradicting my own wording? No -- my exclusion targets new AI-specific legislation (an EO, a state AI-liability statute, a federal moratorium bill), not a court applying pre-existing general law. A copyright, product-liability, or negligence ruling is precisely the 'existing common-law/statutory-but-general' forum my mechanism predicts stays open when Congress doesn't act. I'll also concede a boundary in the other direction: the Anthropic/Bartz authors' settlement (Sept 2025) is money-plus-data-destruction with no deployment change -- that would NOT satisfy my claim, which sharpens rather than weakens the criterion. The mechanism -- harmed parties have nowhere else to go, and judges must rule on pending dockets regardless of legislative gridlock -- doesn't need every case to resolve, just one to bite by mid-2028, and one already has.

body.ruling: Export-control-driven compute constraints will be the only mechanism that visibly and checkably changes a frontier lab's behavior on a dated action in this window, while voluntary safety commitments erode under competitive pressure and litigation/state-level moves are too slow or too indirect to bite by comparable dates.
body.because: ai-regulation-teeth's claim is the only one that names a mechanism with an existing, demonstrated causal channel (export controls have already forced compute/location decisions) and sets a falsification bar that requires comparing it against contracts/insurers/voluntary standards producing zero equivalent instances — this is a stronger, comparative claim than the others' single-event claims. ai-pressure and lab-moves are effectively the same argument (a lab loosening or breaching its own voluntary safety commitment under reputational-only enforcement) reached independently, so they count as one thesis, not two independently corroborating ones. ai-courts-decide and ai-public-backlash both concede in round 2 that their channels (litigation, state infrastructure law) are plausible but slower or narrower than export controls, without landing a rebuttal that beats the export-control claim's specificity and precedent.
body.strongest_minute: ai-regulation-teeth — the only claim built as a comparative/relative test (X will happen, Y and Z will not) rather than a single existence claim, which makes it both riskier to assert and more informative if it holds; it also grounds itself in an already-observed causal mechanism (export controls forcing dated compute/deployment decisions) rather than an extrapolated one.
body.weakest_minute: ai-public-backlash — it retreats from the actual question (what constrains frontier-lab *behavior*) to a claim about state-level data-center infrastructure law, which regulates real estate/utilities, not model behavior, and its round-2 defense against ai-regulation-teeth never establishes that infrastructure statutes change what a lab ships or how.
body.shared_assumption: ai-pressure and lab-moves both assume, without arguing it, that a lab's RSP/Preparedness Framework revision or breach is legible and attributable from the outside on a specific date — i.e., that labs will either announce framework changes clearly or that observers can cleanly detect a 'loosening' relative to a 2025-2026 baseline.
body.unresolved: Whether a lab weakening or bypassing its own voluntary safety framework (ai-pressure/lab-moves) is a materially different, more decision-relevant event than a court forcing a product change (ai-courts-decide) or export controls forcing a compute change (ai-regulation-teeth) — the minutes never rank these against each other on decision-relevance, only on likelihood and checkability.
